how.h: An API is a restaurant menu
how.p: An API (application programming interface) is the menu a restaurant hands you. It lists what you may order, how to phrase the order, and what you will get back. You never walk into the kitchen. Because many different callers will use that menu for years, it has to be clear, stable and safe to repeat.

Most web APIs name things as nouns (`/orders/42`) and use HTTP verbs for the action: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH changes, DELETE removes. The reply carries a status code that tells the caller what happened: 201 created, 400 bad input, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 missing, 429 too many requests. Honest codes let clients react correctly without guessing.

Networks fail in the middle. If you send a payment and the connection drops, you cannot tell whether it was processed. An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. GET and DELETE are idempotent by definition, but POST (create) is not, so APIs add an idempotency key to make it safe.

The client makes a unique random ID for each logical operation and sends it in an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server remembers the key together with the result of the first attempt. If the same key arrives again, the server returns the saved result instead of doing the work again. Stripe describes this exact pattern, and also checks that a reused key comes with the same parameters, so a key is not accidentally reused for a different request.

Never return an unbounded list. Offset pagination (`?page=5`) shifts when rows are added or removed while someone is paging, so items can be skipped or repeated. Cursor pagination hands back a bookmark that points at the last item seen, so it stays stable. Put a version in the URL or a header so you can change the API later, and rate limit callers so one bad client cannot hurt the others.

worked.title: A payment that is retried safely
steps: A client wants to charge 49.99 dollars. It generates the key `k-7f3a-91c2` and sends POST /payments with amount 4999 (cents) and that key.
The server sees the key for the first time, records it as in progress, charges the card once, and saves the response (status 201, payment id p_100) under the key.
The response is lost on the network. The client sees a timeout and does not know if it worked.
The client waits 1 second and retries with the same key and the same body. If it fails again it waits 2 s, then 4 s (exponential backoff), with a little random jitter added.
The server finds the saved result for `k-7f3a-91c2`, sees the parameters match, and returns the stored 201 for p_100 without charging again.
If the client had sent the same key with amount 5999 instead, the server would refuse it as a mismatch.
worked.result: Two requests arrived but the customer was charged exactly once: one payment, 49.99 dollars. Stripe notes that on its v1 API saved keys can be pruned after at least 24 hours, so a key is for retries, not for permanent bookkeeping.

case.title: Making payment retries safe
case.text: Stripe lets clients attach an idempotency key to any POST request. It saves the status code and body of the first request that began executing under that key, and replays them for retries, even if that first result was a server error. Keys can be up to 255 characters and Stripe suggests random V4 UUIDs. The server compares the incoming parameters to the original and errors if they differ, which prevents accidental misuse. Stripe also recommends clients combine keys with exponential backoff and jitter so many clients do not retry at the same instant.

source.title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency

choose: Idempotency key header
Any POST that creates something or moves money
Servers must store keys and results; keys expire, so clients cannot reuse them forever
Natural idempotent design (PUT with a known id)
The client can choose the resource id
Does not help when the server must generate the id
Cursor pagination
Lists that change while users page through them, or are very large
You cannot jump straight to page 50
Offset pagination
Small, rarely changing lists, admin screens
Skipped or repeated rows when data changes, and slow on deep pages
URL versioning (/v1/)
Public APIs with many outside clients
You must run old versions for a long time
mistakes: Retrying a POST without an idempotency key, which risks double charges. Always pair retries with a key on anything that creates or pays.
Using a sensitive value such as an email address as the key. Use a random UUID instead.
Reusing one key for different requests. A key identifies one logical operation only.
Returning 200 with an error message in the body. Use proper status codes so clients and caches behave correctly.
Returning whole lists with no limit. Cap page size and paginate everything.
Changing a field name or meaning inside an existing version. That breaks callers; add a new version instead.

reading.title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency
Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures

how.p: Think of REST as a set menu of fixed dishes at fixed counters, GraphQL as a build-your-own bowl where you list exactly the ingredients you want, and gRPC as a direct phone line to the kitchen with a strict script. All three let one program talk to another. They differ in how much the caller can shape the answer and how efficient the wire format is.

REST was described by Roy Fielding as a set of constraints: client and server are separate, every request carries everything needed to understand it (stateless), responses say whether they can be cached, and all resources share one uniform interface. Statelessness helps servers scale and recover. The price is that each request repeats some data, and a generic interface is less tailored to any one screen.

how.h: GraphQL: the client picks the fields
how.p: GraphQL exposes one endpoint and a typed schema. The client sends a query naming exactly the fields it wants, even across related objects, and gets back just those fields in one round trip. This avoids over-fetching (receiving fields you never use) and under-fetching (needing a second call). The cost moves to the server: a nested query can be very expensive, so servers must limit depth and cost.

how.h: gRPC: typed calls with generated code
how.p: In gRPC you describe services and message shapes in a `.proto` file using Protocol Buffers, a compact binary format. A compiler then generates client and server code in many languages, so calling a remote method feels like calling a local one. It suits internal service-to-service calls where speed and strict contracts matter. Browsers cannot call it directly without a proxy.

Ask who the callers are. Unknown outside developers want something simple, cacheable and easy to try with a browser or curl, which is REST. Many different client screens with different data needs fit GraphQL. Your own services talking to each other thousands of times a second fit gRPC. Many companies use more than one style side by side.

worked.title: Pricing a GraphQL query before you allow it
steps: GitHub rates GraphQL queries by points. Take a query asking for 100 repositories, each with 50 issues, each issue with 60 labels.
Count the requests the server would need: 1 for the repositories list, plus 100 for each repository's issues, plus 100 x 50 = 5,000 for each issue's labels. Total 1 + 100 + 5,000 = 5,101.
GitHub divides by 100 and rounds, so the cost is about 51 points.
A normal user gets 5,000 points per hour. 5,000 / 51 is about 98, so roughly 98 such queries per hour.
Compare REST: the same data would be about 5,101 separate HTTP calls if you fetched each list yourself.
GitHub also caps one call at 500,000 total nodes and requires every list to ask for between 1 and 100 items.
worked.result: One 51-point query replaces thousands of REST calls, but the server must price and cap queries, otherwise a single deeply nested request can do enormous work.

case.title: Adding GraphQL next to REST
case.text: GitHub introduced its GraphQL API in 2016 because of problems with REST. It reported that REST made up over 60 percent of requests to its database tier, and clients often needed two or three calls to assemble one view while still receiving data they did not need. GraphQL let clients request exact fields in one query and gave GitHub a strict type system, introspection and the ability to check things like OAuth scopes before running a query. Today GitHub still offers both styles, and it protects GraphQL with point-based rate limits and node limits.

choose: REST
Public or partner APIs, simple CRUD, anything that benefits from HTTP caching
Chatty for complex screens; endpoints can return too much or too little
GraphQL
Many client types such as mobile and web with different data needs
Expensive nested queries need cost limits; HTTP caching is harder
gRPC
Internal service-to-service calls where speed and strict contracts matter
Binary payloads are harder to debug by hand; browsers need a proxy
REST outside, gRPC inside
A gateway exposes simple REST while services talk gRPC behind it
Two contracts to keep in sync
mistakes: Exposing GraphQL with no depth, node or cost limits. Price queries up front and cap them.
Choosing GraphQL only because it is fashionable when one client and a few endpoints would do.
Calling every HTTP+JSON API 'REST' and ignoring status codes, caching headers and statelessness.
Changing field numbers in a `.proto` file. Protobuf identifies fields by number, so reuse or renumbering breaks old clients.
Putting gRPC directly in front of browsers without a translating proxy.
Forgetting that GraphQL still needs authorisation checks on every field, not only at the front door.

reading.title: Rate limits and query limits for the GraphQL API
Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, chapter 5 (REST)

how.p: An API gateway is the reception desk of a hotel. Guests (clients) talk to one desk instead of knocking on every room. The desk checks who you are, sends your request to the right room, and sometimes gathers several answers into one. Behind it, rooms can be renovated or moved without guests noticing.

The gateway is the single entry point for all clients. It forwards a request to the correct service, or fans out to several services and combines the replies. It can also handle shared jobs such as checking authentication, rate limiting and translating between a public protocol and whatever services use internally. Chris Richardson lists the benefits as hiding how the system is split, giving each client a tailored API, and saving round trips on slow mobile networks.

The gateway is one more component to build, deploy and keep running, and it adds a network hop. If it holds too much business logic it becomes a bottleneck for every team. A common variation, Backends for Frontends, gives each client type (web, mobile) its own small gateway so teams do not fight over one.

In a cloud system service instances come and go, so their addresses keep changing. Service discovery lets callers find a healthy instance by name. In Kubernetes a Service object gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name, and a controller keeps the list of matching pods (found through label selectors) up to date automatically. Outside Kubernetes a registry such as Consul or Eureka plays the same role.

Martin Fowler named this after strangler fig vines that grow around a host tree until they can stand alone. Instead of a risky big-bang rewrite, you put a router (often the gateway) in front of the old system and move one capability at a time to new code. Each moved route sends traffic to the new service while everything else still goes to the old one. When nothing is left behind, you switch off the old system.

worked.title: Fan-out versus three calls, then a gradual cutover
steps: A mobile home screen needs profile, orders and recommendations. Each service takes about 40 ms (illustrative numbers). Sequentially from the phone over a 100 ms mobile round trip each, that is 3 x 100 = 300 ms of network plus 3 x 40 = 120 ms of work.

With a gateway, the phone makes one call (100 ms round trip). The gateway calls the three services in parallel inside the data centre, so it waits about the slowest one, around 40 ms, plus a few ms to combine them.
The user waits roughly 100 + 45 = 145 ms instead of about 420 ms.

Now migrate with a strangler. The monolith serves /search. The router is set to send 5 percent of /search traffic to a new search service: at 1,000 requests per minute that is 50 to the new one and 950 to the old.
Errors look fine, so raise to 25 percent (250 per minute), then 100 percent, then delete the old search code. If errors spike at any step, set the percentage back to 0.
worked.result: The gateway cut waiting from about 420 ms to about 145 ms in this example, and the strangler approach moved a feature with the ability to roll back at every step.

case.title: Naming the strangler fig
case.text: Fowler first wrote about the idea in 2001 after seeing strangler figs in the rainforests of Queensland, Australia. He argues that full rewrites often fail because they take too long and recreate behaviour nobody wants, so teams should build new functionality alongside the legacy system and move behaviour over gradually. His advice includes agreeing on outcomes early, expecting that seams in old code are hard to find, delivering small pieces early, and accepting that temporary transitional code is a cost worth paying. He also stresses that the organisation must change, otherwise the new system tends to look like the old one.

choose: Single API gateway
A small to medium number of services and similar clients
Can become a bottleneck and a release choke point
Backends for Frontends
Web, mobile and partner clients that need very different shapes of data
More gateways to run; some duplicated logic
Kubernetes Service DNS
You already run on Kubernetes
Tied to that platform; across clusters you need more
Registry such as Consul or Eureka
Mixed environments or VMs
A registry is another critical system to keep healthy
Strangler fig
Replacing a legacy system you cannot stop
You live with two systems and transitional code for a while
mistakes: Putting business logic in the gateway until it becomes a mini monolith. Keep it to routing, auth, limits and light composition.
Running a single gateway instance. It is the front door, so run several behind a load balancer.
Hard-coding service addresses. Use discovery so instances can move.
Starting a strangler migration without a way to route back. Keep rollback to the old path at every step.
Migrating the data last. Plan early how data will be split, because shared databases tie old and new together.
Skipping health checks, so the gateway keeps sending traffic to dead instances.

reading.title: Pattern: API Gateway / Backends for Frontends

how.h: One big kitchen or many food stalls
how.p: A monolith is one big kitchen where every cook works in the same room on the same menu. Microservices are a food court of separate stalls, each with its own staff and recipes. The food court lets stalls change independently, but customers now need to walk between stalls and someone has to keep the whole court running.

Fowler and Lewis describe them as services that run as separate processes, are deployed independently and are organised around business capabilities, such as orders or payments. Each service usually owns its own data and talks to others through simple protocols such as HTTP APIs or messages. Teams own their service from build to running it in production.

Every call between services crosses a network and can fail or be slow, so you need timeouts, retries and fallbacks. You can no longer rely on one database transaction across services, so you accept eventual consistency and use compensating steps to fix mistakes. You also need deep investment in monitoring, logging, automated deployment and tracing.

Fowler's MonolithFirst argument is that early on you do not yet know whether anyone wants your product, and you do not yet know where the natural boundaries lie. Moving code between services is much harder than moving it inside one program. So build a well-structured monolith, learn the boundaries, and split only when a clear reason appears, such as a team that must deploy independently.

Splitting helps when many teams collide in one codebase, when one part needs very different scaling, or when a part needs different technology. It does not help a small team with an unclear product. A middle path is a modular monolith with strict internal boundaries, which can be cut apart later.

worked.title: How a chain of services lowers availability
steps: Suppose a checkout request must call 5 services one after another, and each is available 99.9 percent of the time (illustrative).
A request succeeds only if all five are up. Multiply: 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 = about 0.99501.
So the combined availability is about 99.50 percent, not 99.9 percent.
Over a 30-day month, which has 43,200 minutes, 0.1 percent downtime is 43.2 minutes for one service.
The chain's downtime is about 0.499 percent of 43,200, roughly 216 minutes, about five times worse.
Fixes: make some calls asynchronous, add fallbacks for non-essential services, and cut the number of services in the critical path.
worked.result: Five 99.9 percent services in a row give about 99.5 percent, around 216 minutes of trouble a month instead of 43. This is the 'downtime multiplication' Fowler warns about.

case.title: Video quality monitoring moved back into one process
case.text: In 2023 the Prime Video team published how its audio and video monitoring service, which checks streams for quality problems, was rebuilt. The first design spread work across separate components and stored intermediate frames in Amazon S3 between steps, which added cost and limits at scale. The team put the components into a single process running as an Amazon ECS task and reported a cost reduction of over 90 percent along with better scaling. Commentators point out that this was one narrow service and not all of Prime Video, so it is a lesson about matching architecture to workload, not a verdict against microservices.

source.title: Scaling up the Prime Video audio/video monitoring service and reducing costs by 90%

choose: Modular monolith
A new product, a small team, boundaries still unclear
Needs discipline to keep module boundaries clean
Microservices
Many teams, parts that scale or release independently
Network failures, eventual consistency, large operational burden
A few coarse services
A middle path when one or two parts clearly need to be separate
Boundaries may still need to move later
Strangler fig split
An existing monolith that has become a bottleneck
You run two systems during the migration
mistakes: Starting with dozens of tiny services before the product or boundaries are known. Start modular and split later.
Sharing one database between services, which silently couples them. Give each service its own data.
Long synchronous chains of calls, which multiply failures. Prefer events or fewer hops.
Splitting by technical layer (UI service, database service) instead of by business capability.
Having no tracing or central logging before splitting. You will not be able to debug one request across services.
Treating microservices as a goal. They are a tool for team scaling, and sometimes merging services back is the right call.

reading.title: Microservices: a definition of this new architectural term

how.h: A noticeboard instead of a phone call
how.p: With request/response you phone someone and wait for an answer. With events you pin a note on a noticeboard saying what happened, such as OrderPlaced, and anyone interested reads it when they can. The sender no longer needs to know who reads it, and a slow reader does not stop the sender.

A service publishes an event, a fact in the past tense, to a broker such as Kafka or a message queue. Other services subscribe and react: email sends a receipt, inventory reserves stock, analytics counts the sale. New consumers can be added without changing the producer. The trade-off is eventual consistency, meaning other services catch up a moment later.

A service often must update its database and publish an event, and doing both reliably is hard: publish first and the database write may fail, write first and the process may crash before publishing. The outbox pattern writes the event into an outbox table inside the same database transaction as the business change. A separate relay reads the outbox and publishes. Because the relay can crash after publishing but before marking the row done, duplicates can occur, so consumers must be idempotent, for example by remembering the event ids they have processed.

Normally you store only the current state. In event sourcing you store every change as an event in an ordered log and compute the current state by replaying them. You get a full audit trail and can rebuild state as of any past moment or create new views later. To avoid replaying a huge history you save periodic snapshots and replay only newer events.

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) uses one model for writes (commands) and separate model(s) for reads (queries), possibly on different hardware. It helps when reads and writes are very unbalanced or when one model has become too convoluted. Fowler warns it is a significant mental shift, suits only specific parts of a system, and has caused serious trouble when used where plain CRUD would do.

worked.title: Event log, snapshot and a duplicate event
steps: An account's events in order: Deposited 100, Withdrew 30, Deposited 50, Withdrew 20.
Replay from zero: 0 + 100 = 100, then 70, then 120, then 100. The current balance is 100.
Take a snapshot after event 2: balance 70. After a restart, load the snapshot and replay only events 3 and 4: 70 + 50 = 120, then 120 - 20 = 100. Same answer, two events replayed instead of four.
Now the outbox: placing order 555 inserts one order row and one outbox row (event id E-9001) in the same transaction. Both commit or neither does.
The relay publishes E-9001, then crashes before marking it sent. After restart it publishes E-9001 again.
The email service keeps a set of processed event ids. On the second E-9001 it sees the id and skips it.
worked.result: Replay gave balance 100 either way, and the customer got one receipt even though the event was delivered twice. Atomic outbox writes plus idempotent consumers are what make it reliable.

case.who: Event sourcing as described by Martin Fowler
case.title: What a log of events buys you and costs you
case.text: Fowler's write-up of event sourcing says the main benefits are a complete audit trail, the ability to reconstruct past states, replaying real events in a test environment to check an upgrade, and building new applications by consuming the same stream. It also lists real drawbacks: the style is unfamiliar to many developers, external systems complicate replay (you must not send emails again while replaying), changing code over old events is harder, read models can lag behind, and retrofitting event sourcing into an existing system is difficult. The takeaway is to choose it early, deliberately and only where the history is valuable.

choose: Plain request/response
The caller needs the answer now
Caller is blocked and fails when the callee is down
Publish/subscribe events
Several services react to one fact; you want to absorb spikes
Eventual consistency, harder to trace the flow
Outbox pattern
You must change the database and publish an event reliably
Needs a relay and idempotent consumers because of duplicates
CQRS
Reads and writes are very different in shape or scale
Extra complexity; most systems do not need it
Event sourcing
Audit history and replay are core requirements
Hard to change later; event schema versioning is a long-term task
mistakes: Publishing the event outside the database transaction. Use an outbox or equivalent.
Assuming each event arrives exactly once. Design consumers to handle duplicates.
Using events as remote procedure calls (a command disguised as an event). Events state facts, they do not order work.
Adopting CQRS or event sourcing for a simple CRUD screen.
Putting huge payloads in events instead of ids and key fields, which makes versioning painful.
Forgetting to monitor consumer lag, so a stuck consumer goes unnoticed.

how.p: A house has fuses so one faulty appliance trips its own circuit instead of burning down the building. A car has a spare tyre so one puncture does not end the trip. Resilience patterns do the same for software: they assume every dependency will sometimes be slow or down, and keep the rest of the system alive.

A call with no timeout can wait forever, and waiting threads pile up until the caller itself dies. AWS suggests picking an acceptable rate of false timeouts, such as 0.1 percent, and setting the timeout near the downstream service's latency at that percentile (p99.9). Include connection setup in your thinking: one AWS example had a 20 ms timeout that failed after deployments because new TLS connections took longer.

Retries fix short blips but are selfish: they spend more of the server's capacity to help one request. Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure, for example about 0.2 s, 0.4 s, 0.8 s. Jitter adds randomness so thousands of clients that failed together do not retry together. Retry at only one layer of the system, otherwise attempts multiply.

A circuit breaker counts failures. When they pass a threshold it opens and calls fail immediately without touching the struggling service. After a pause it goes half-open and lets one trial call through: success closes it, failure keeps it open. Bulkheads, named after ship compartments, give each dependency its own pool of threads or connections so one slow dependency cannot use them all.

Decide in advance what the user sees when a part fails. If recommendations are down, show the page without them. A fallback that is slightly worse beats an error page. Make sure retried operations are idempotent, otherwise a retry can repeat a side effect such as a charge.

worked.title: Choosing a timeout and counting retry load
steps: Your service calls a database. Its latency at p99.9 is 300 ms (illustrative). Set the timeout to 300 ms, accepting that 0.1 percent of calls will time out falsely.
At 1,000 requests per second, 0.1 percent is about 1 false timeout per second, which a single retry covers cheaply.
Backoff with full jitter: after failure n wait a random time between 0 and min(cap, 0.2 x 2^n). Upper bounds are 0.2 s, 0.4 s, 0.8 s, 1.6 s. Two clients rarely pick the same instant.
Danger case: 5 layers of services, each making up to 3 attempts. Worst case the bottom database sees 3 x 3 x 3 x 3 x 3 = 243 times the normal load, the figure AWS gives.
Fix it by retrying only at the top layer, and add a retry budget so retries stop when many calls are failing.
Add a circuit breaker with, for example, a threshold of 5 consecutive failures and a short reset period before a trial call.
worked.result: With a sensible timeout, jittered backoff and a single retry layer, a blip is invisible to users. Without those, the same blip becomes a 243-fold load spike that keeps the database down.

case.title: Retries that help, and retries that hurt
case.text: In the Amazon Builders' Library, AWS describes how it uses timeouts, retries and jittered backoff. It stresses that retries are selfish and can prolong an overload, that stacked retries multiply load, and that jitter is needed to stop clients from synchronising. For limiting retries, it argues that circuit breakers are hard to test and slow recovery, and prefers a local token bucket so a client can retry freely while tokens remain and falls to a slow, fixed retry rate once they run out. The AWS SDK added this behaviour in 2016. It also warns that retrying is only safe when operations are idempotent.

source.title: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter

choose: Timeouts
Every remote call, always
Too short causes false failures; too long ties up resources
Retry with backoff and jitter
Transient errors on idempotent operations
Multiplies load when stacked; needs idempotency
Circuit breaker
A dependency that can fail for a long time
More states to tune and test; trips can hide real problems if not monitored
Retry budget (token bucket)
Many clients, risk of retry storms
Needs per-client tuning
Bulkhead
One slow dependency could starve unrelated work
Smaller pools mean some capacity sits idle
mistakes: Calls with no timeout, or the library default of 'wait forever'. Set explicit connect and read timeouts.
Retrying immediately in a tight loop. Always back off with jitter.
Retrying at every layer. Choose one layer to retry, and fail fast in the rest.
Retrying non-idempotent operations without a key. Make them safe first.
A circuit breaker nobody monitors. Log state changes and alert when one trips.
No fallback plan, so any single failure becomes a visible outage. Decide what a degraded page looks like.

how.p: Imagine an arcade machine that gives you a bucket holding up to 10 tokens. Every game costs one token, and a staff member drops in 5 new tokens each second until the bucket is full. You can play 10 games in a burst, but over a long time you cannot beat 5 games per second. That is a token bucket.

Each client has a bucket with a capacity and a refill rate. When a request arrives, you first add tokens for the time that has passed since you last looked (rate times elapsed seconds, never above capacity). If at least one token is available, you remove it and allow the request. Otherwise you reject it with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, optionally with a `Retry-After` header saying how long to wait.

how.h: Keeping state in the right place
how.p: One server can keep buckets in memory, but a fleet of servers must share counts, otherwise a client simply spreads requests across servers. Stripe keeps its limiter state in Redis, an in-memory data store. Because many requests update the same bucket at once, the read-update-write must be atomic, for example by using a Redis script or a lock.

Stripe describes four kinds. A request rate limiter caps requests per second per user. A concurrent requests limiter caps how many are in flight at once. A fleet usage load shedder reserves capacity for critical traffic and rejects less important traffic when the system is busy. A worker utilization shedder is a last line of defence that sheds low-priority work, starting with test mode traffic, when workers are nearly full.

A limiter is itself a dependency, so make it fail open: if the limiter or Redis is down, let requests through. Return clear errors, add kill switches and metrics, and dark launch a new limiter (log what it would block before enforcing). Change limits gradually, because Stripe found fast changes make the system flap between good and bad states.

worked.title: A bucket of 10 refilling at 5 per second
steps: Capacity is 10 tokens and the refill rate is 5 tokens per second. The bucket starts full with 10.
At t = 0 a client sends 10 requests at once. Each takes a token, all 10 pass, and the bucket is empty.
An 11th request at t = 0 finds no token and gets 429.
At t = 0.4 s the bucket has refilled 0.4 x 5 = 2 tokens. Two requests pass, a third is rejected.
At t = 2 s of idle time, the bucket refills to 2 x 5 = 10 tokens, back at capacity (it never goes above 10).
Over any full minute, the most this client can get through is the starting burst plus the refill: 10 + 5 x 60 = 310 requests.
worked.result: The client may burst 10 requests instantly, but long-term traffic is held to 5 per second, about 300 a minute, plus the one-time burst of 10.

case.title: Four layers of rate limiting and load shedding
case.text: Stripe's engineering post explains that it runs a request rate limiter, a concurrent requests limiter, a fleet usage load shedder and a worker utilization load shedder, and that the rate limiter uses the token bucket idea with state in Redis. Its lessons are practical: fail open, return actionable errors, build in kill switches and metrics, dark launch each limiter, and shed and restore load gradually to avoid flapping. Stripe also advises starting with just a request rate limiter and adding the others as your scale demands them.

source.title: Scaling your API with rate limiters

choose: Token bucket
You want to allow short bursts but cap the average rate
Needs atomic updates when shared; two numbers to tune
Fixed window counter
Very simple limits where precision is not important
Allows a double burst at the window edge
Sliding window
You need a smoother, fairer limit
Uses more memory or more calculation
Concurrency limit
Requests are expensive and the real risk is too many at once
Needs careful tracking when requests end abnormally
Load shedding
The whole system is overloaded and must protect critical work
You must define which traffic is critical
mistakes: Keeping buckets in each server's memory in a multi-server system, so the real limit is multiplied by the number of servers.
A non-atomic read-then-write on the shared counter, which lets a burst slip through. Use an atomic operation.
Failing closed when the limiter store is down, which turns a Redis outage into a full API outage.
Returning 429 with no hint. Send `Retry-After` and a clear message.
Using the same limit for every client and every endpoint. Heavy endpoints need tighter limits.
Enabling a new limit without a dark launch, then discovering it blocks real customers.

how.h: A car dashboard plus a black box
how.p: A car dashboard shows speed and engine temperature right now, while a flight recorder lets investigators replay what happened. Observability gives you both for software. It means you can understand what is going on inside a system by asking questions from the outside, even about problems you never predicted.

Metrics are numbers aggregated over time, such as requests per second or error rate, and they tell you whether the service is healthy. Logs are timestamped messages that record what happened, most useful when structured and tagged with a request id. Traces follow a single request across many services: each step is a span with a name and timing, and the spans nest under a root span that covers the whole request.

When a request enters, it gets a trace id. Each service passes that id on to the services it calls, which is called context propagation. Every service records spans carrying the same id, and a backend stitches them together into a waterfall view. Google's Dapper paper showed this can be done with low overhead by sampling and by instrumenting only common shared libraries.

Google's SRE book names four golden signals: latency (track successful and failed requests separately), traffic, errors and saturation (how full your resources are). Use percentiles, because averages hide a slow tail. Page humans on symptoms users feel, and use cause-level data for debugging.

Alert only when a human needs to act, otherwise people learn to ignore alerts. Prefer alerts tied to your service level objective, such as how fast you are using up your error budget. Alongside monitoring, keep a ladder of tests: many fast unit tests, integration tests against real databases, a few end-to-end tests, and load tests before launches.

worked.title: Reading a trace and a percentile
steps: A checkout request takes 480 ms in total. The trace shows a root span of 480 ms with three sequential children (illustrative numbers): gateway 20 ms, orders service 110 ms, payments service 350 ms. 20 + 110 + 350 = 480.
Inside payments, a child span shows 300 ms waiting for the external card provider.
300 / 480 = 62.5 percent of the whole request is that one external call. That is where to look first.
Now the metrics side: out of 1,000 requests, 980 take 100 ms and 20 take 3,000 ms.
Mean latency = (980 x 100 + 20 x 3,000) / 1,000 = (98,000 + 60,000) / 1,000 = 158 ms. That looks acceptable.
The 99th percentile is 3,000 ms, because the slowest 20 requests are 2 percent of the traffic, more than the 1 percent that p99 ignores.
worked.result: The trace pinpointed the card provider as 62.5 percent of the latency, and the percentile showed a 3-second tail that a 158 ms average would have hidden.

case.title: Dapper: tracing at the scale of thousands of machines
case.text: Google's Dapper paper reports more than two years of running a production tracing system across a huge fleet. The goals were low overhead, application-level transparency (developers should not have to change their code) and deployment everywhere. Google got there with sampling and by instrumenting a small set of common libraries. Dapper started as a standalone tracing tool and grew into a monitoring platform that supported many analysis tools, some its designers had not anticipated. The lesson is that traces become far more useful when they are built in everywhere, not added to one service at a time.

source.title: Dapper, a large-scale distributed systems tracing infrastructure

mistakes: Alerting on every CPU spike. Page on user-visible symptoms and keep cause metrics for dashboards.
Watching only averages. Track p95 and p99 as well.
Unstructured log lines with no request id, making it impossible to follow one request.
Tracing only some services, so traces break in the middle. Propagate the trace id everywhere.

how.h: A school report with a pass mark
how.p: An SLI (service level indicator) is a measurement, like your test score. An SLO (service level objective) is the pass mark you aim for. An SLA (service level agreement) is a contract that says what happens if you fail, such as refunds. If missing the target has no explicit penalty, it is an SLO, not an SLA.

Pick a few measurements that reflect what users care about: for a serving system that is usually availability, latency and throughput, and for storage it adds durability. Start from user needs and work back to something measurable, not the reverse. Use percentiles, for example 99 percent of requests faster than 300 ms, because averages hide slow requests.

Do not just adopt today's performance as the target, and do not promise perfection. Google's guidance is to keep the number of SLOs small, drop any that never influence decisions, and start looser and tighten later because relaxing an unattainable target is hard. Keep an internal target stricter than the one you publish, to leave a safety margin.

The error budget is the amount of failure the SLO allows. A 99.9 percent target means 0.1 percent of requests may fail, and this budget is spent by incidents, bad releases and maintenance. While budget remains, teams can ship fast. When it runs out, reliability work takes priority over new features. Because each extra nine can cost far more than the last, the goal is the right level of reliability, not 100 percent.

A burn rate of 1 means you will use exactly the whole budget by the end of the window. Alerting on burn rate means each alert corresponds to a meaningful chunk of lost budget. The Google SRE Workbook suggests using a long and a short window together: the long one gives precision and the short one makes the alert reset quickly once the problem stops.

worked.title: Turning 99.9 percent into minutes and alerts
steps: A 30-day month has 30 x 24 x 60 = 43,200 minutes.
A 99.9 percent SLO allows 0.1 percent downtime: 43,200 x 0.001 = 43.2 minutes. A 99.99 percent SLO allows 4.32 minutes.
By requests: with 10 million requests a month, 0.1 percent is 10,000 failed requests allowed.
An outage of 10 minutes uses 10 / 43.2 = about 23 percent of the monthly budget.
Burn rate: if 1.44 percent of requests fail, you are failing at 1.44 / 0.1 = 14.4 times the allowed rate.
At 14.4x for 1 hour you consume 14.4 x 1 / 720 hours = 2 percent of the 30-day budget. The SRE Workbook uses this as a paging threshold, with a 5-minute short window.
worked.result: 99.9 percent means about 43 minutes of failure a month, and a sustained 14.4x burn is the speed at which 2 percent of that budget disappears in one hour, a good point to page a human.

case.title: Using the error budget to settle release arguments
case.text: Google's SRE book explains that product and SRE teams agree an SLO, a neutral monitoring system measures real performance, and the gap is the remaining budget. When budget remains, releases continue; when incidents drain it, releases slow or pause while the team invests in testing and resilience. This turns a political fight between 'ship faster' and 'be safer' into a shared number. The book also notes that each extra nine of availability can cost around 100 times more, that users often cannot perceive the difference at very high levels, and that a team struggling to ship may loosen its SLO to create room to innovate.

choose: 99 percent
Internal tools, batch jobs, early products
Allows about 7.2 hours of failure in 30 days, which is far too loose for customer-facing paths
99.9 percent
Most customer-facing web services
About 43 minutes a month leaves little room for slow, manual recovery
99.99 percent
Payments, core platform services
About 4.3 minutes a month needs automation, redundancy and a large engineering investment
Latency SLO with percentiles
User-facing interactions where speed matters
Needs good measurement of the whole distribution, not the mean
SLA with penalties
Contracts with paying customers
Set it looser than your internal SLO; public promises are hard to change
mistakes: Setting 100 percent. It is impossible and the cost is unbounded. Pick a number users can actually perceive.
Measuring only what is easy, such as server CPU, instead of what users experience.
Using averages for latency SLOs. Use percentiles.
Publishing an SLA identical to the internal SLO. Keep a safety margin.
Alerting on every dip rather than on budget burn, which creates noise.
Having an error budget with no consequence. Agree in advance what happens when the budget is spent.

reading.title: SRE fundamentals: SLIs, SLAs and SLOs

how.p: A fire drill lets a building practise an evacuation before there is a real fire. Chaos engineering does the same for software: you deliberately cause small, controlled failures so you find weaknesses on your own terms, not at 3 a.m. during a real outage.

The Principles of Chaos Engineering describe an experiment as four moves. Define the steady state as a measurable output, such as orders per minute. Hypothesise that it will hold in both a control group and an experimental group. Introduce realistic disruptions such as a crashed server or a cut network connection. Look for a difference between the groups. The harder it is to disturb the steady state, the more confidence you gain.

Measure outputs users care about, not internal mechanics. Vary real-world events, from hardware failure to traffic spikes. Experiments are most informative in production because that is where the real traffic is, but you must minimise the blast radius, which means starting tiny, such as one instance or a small percentage of users, and keep a quick way to stop. Over time, automate the experiments so they run continuously.

When a real incident happens, appoint an incident commander who coordinates and a communicator who updates stakeholders. Mitigate first by rolling back, failing over or shedding load, and look for the root cause after users are safe. Keep a timeline as you go because memory is unreliable afterwards.

A postmortem is a written record of the impact, timeline, how it was mitigated, root causes and follow-up actions. It must be blameless: Google's SRE guidance assumes everyone acted in good faith with the information they had, and looks for gaps in systems and processes. Blame makes people hide problems, which makes the next incident worse. Track the action items until they are done.

worked.title: A first chaos experiment on a web tier
steps: Setup: 12 identical instances, each handling about 100 requests per second. Normal traffic is 900 requests per second, so utilisation is 900 / 1,200 = 75 percent. Steady state: p99 latency under 400 ms and error rate under 0.1 percent (illustrative targets).
Hypothesis: if one instance is killed, the steady state holds.
Blast radius: terminate exactly 1 instance of 12, about 8.3 percent of capacity, during business hours with engineers watching.
Predict: 11 instances give 1,100 requests per second of capacity, so utilisation rises to 900 / 1,100 = about 81.8 percent. That should be fine.
Run it. Suppose p99 latency stays at 380 ms and errors at 0.02 percent: hypothesis confirmed.

Widen the experiment: kill 3 instances. Now capacity is 9 x 100 = 900, utilisation hits 100 percent and latency will climb, so you learn you need autoscaling or more headroom before you try that in production.
worked.result: One failure is survivable at 81.8 percent utilisation. Losing three would saturate the fleet, a weakness found safely with a plan to fix it.

case.title: Chaos Monkey: killing instances on purpose
case.text: Netflix built Chaos Monkey, which randomly terminates instances in production so that engineers are pushed to build services that keep working when any single instance disappears. It is released as part of Netflix open source software and works with the Spinnaker deployment platform, where each application can customise how the tool treats it. The wider practice was formalised in the Principles of Chaos Engineering, which stress steady-state measurements, realistic failures, production experiments, automation and a small blast radius. The lasting lesson is cultural: if failure is normal and constant, nobody can build something that depends on an instance staying alive.

choose: Game day (scheduled drill)
Your first chaos work, practising incident response with the whole team
Needs planning; only tests what you think to rehearse
Instance or pod kill
Verifying redundancy and auto-recovery
Does not test slow dependencies or partial failures
Latency injection
Checking timeouts, retries and breakers
Can cause real customer impact if the blast radius is large
Staging environment experiments
Early confidence before touching production
Traffic and data differ from production, so findings can mislead
Continuous automated chaos
Mature teams with strong monitoring and rollback
Needs automation, kill switches and a team culture that accepts it
mistakes: Running chaos with no defined steady state, so you cannot tell whether it hurt. Write the metric and threshold first.
Starting with a huge blast radius. Begin with one instance or a tiny slice of users.
Running experiments with no abort switch or without people watching.
Skipping incident roles, so everyone investigates and nobody communicates. Name a commander and a communicator.
Hunting for the root cause before mitigating. Roll back or fail over first.
Writing postmortems that blame a person, or that list actions nobody owns or tracks.

reading.title: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software
Chaos Engineering (IEEE Software, 2016)
reading.by: Basiri, Behnam, de Rooij, Hochstein, Kosewski, Reynolds, Rosenthal

how.p: Authentication is showing your ticket at the gate to prove who you are. After that, staff give you a wristband so you do not have to show the ticket again at every tent. In web systems the wristband is a session id or a token. The hard parts are issuing it safely and taking it back.

Never store passwords in plain text or with a fast hash such as SHA-256. Use a slow hash designed for passwords, with a unique random salt per user. OWASP's current first choice is Argon2id, with minimums such as 19 MiB of memory and 2 iterations. Bcrypt is acceptable for legacy systems with a work factor of at least 10. Salts are not secret, and a separate secret pepper kept outside the database adds another layer.

With a server session the server keeps the user's state, often in Redis, and gives the browser a random session id in a cookie. OWASP says the id needs at least 64 bits of entropy and recommends marking the cookie `Secure` (HTTPS only), `HttpOnly` (hidden from scripts) and `SameSite`. Issue a new id after login to prevent session fixation, set idle and absolute timeouts, and on logout destroy the session on the server. Revoking is easy because you delete the server-side record.

A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact string made of a header, a set of claims (such as `iss` issuer, `sub` subject, `aud` audience and `exp` expiry) and a signature. Any service that knows the key can verify it without calling a central server, which suits mobile apps and service-to-service calls. The catch is that a token is valid until it expires, so revocation is hard. Use short lifetimes, and always check the signature, `exp` and `aud`; the algorithm your app accepts is your choice, not the token's.

OAuth 2.0 lets a user grant an app limited access without sharing a password. In the authorisation code flow, the app sends the user to the authorisation server, the user approves, the server redirects back with a short-lived code, and the app exchanges the code for an access token. Prefer a managed login provider over building your own. Learn the standard attacks such as SQL injection (defend with parameterised queries), cross-site scripting and cross-site request forgery, and use the OWASP Top 10 as your checklist.

worked.title: A safe login from start to logout
steps: The user submits an email and password over HTTPS. The server looks up the stored Argon2id hash and its salt, hashes the submitted password the same way, and compares the two.
The match succeeds. The server creates a brand-new session id from a secure random generator. A 16-byte id is 128 bits, written as 32 hex characters, well above the 64-bit minimum.
It stores the session in Redis with a 30 minute idle timeout and an 8 hour absolute timeout (illustrative values within OWASP's examples).
The cookie is sent as `__Host-sid` with `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite=Strict`.

Slow hashing math: if one hash takes about 100 ms (Dropbox reports roughly that for its bcrypt step), one CPU core can test about 10 guesses per second. Trying a list of 1,000,000 common passwords would take 100,000 seconds on that core, over a day, instead of a blink with a fast hash.
On logout the server deletes the session record. Deleting only the browser cookie would leave a stolen copy of the id usable.
worked.result: The user is logged in with an unguessable, correctly flagged session, and password theft from the database is much more expensive to exploit because each guess costs about 100 ms.

case.title: Layers around stored passwords
case.text: Dropbox describes three layers for password storage. First it computes a SHA-512 hash of the password so very long inputs cannot hit bcrypt's input limits. Next it applies bcrypt with a per-user salt at cost factor 10, which takes about 100 ms on its servers. Finally it encrypts the result with AES-256 using a secret key stored separately from the database, a pepper, so a leaked database alone is of little use. It chose encryption over hashing for the last step because the key can be rotated. Dropbox said it would consider moving to argon2 later, and also relies on rate limiting and abuse controls against online guessing.

source.title: How Dropbox securely stores your passwords

Managed login (OAuth, OpenID, passkeys)

bcrypt
Existing systems where bcrypt is already in place

mistakes: Storing passwords with a fast hash or without a unique salt. Use Argon2id or bcrypt with per-user salts.
Keeping the old session id after login, which allows session fixation. Always issue a new id.
Putting a JWT in a place scripts can read while never expiring it. Use short lifetimes and secure storage.
Accepting any JWT algorithm the token asks for, or skipping `exp` and `aud` checks. Validate everything.
Building string-concatenated SQL. Use parameterised queries.
Only deleting the client cookie on logout. Invalidate the session on the server too.

reading.title: How Dropbox securely stores your passwords

how.h: A building with sealed envelopes and keycards
how.p: Imagine a company building. Letters travel in sealed envelopes so couriers cannot read them (encryption in transit). Valuables sit in locked safes (encryption at rest). Rooms are separated, and your keycard opens only the doors your job needs (least privilege). Zero trust adds a guard at every door, even inside the building.

TLS (Transport Layer Security) is what makes HTTPS secure. It gives confidentiality (nobody can read the data), integrity (nobody can change it unnoticed) and authentication (the server proves who it is using a certificate signed by a certificate authority). At the start of a connection, client and server agree on a TLS version, choose algorithms, authenticate the server and agree a secret session key. Use TLS 1.3 where possible and send an HSTS header so browsers always use HTTPS.

how.h: Encryption at rest and key management
how.p: Disks, databases and storage buckets should be encrypted, with the keys held in a key management service rather than next to the data. Rotate keys regularly so a leaked key has a limited lifespan. Keep passwords, tokens and API keys in a secrets manager instead of in source code or container images.

A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your private slice of a cloud network. Put only load balancers in public subnets, and put applications and databases in private subnets with no direct route from the internet. Security groups act as firewalls for each resource and should allow only the necessary ports and sources, for example the database accepts connections only from the app tier.

Traditional security trusted anything inside the network perimeter. NIST's zero trust guidance says to give no implicit trust based on network location, and to authenticate and authorise the user and device before each session. Google's BeyondCorp applied this by making access depend on user and device, not on being on a privileged internal network. Between services, mutual TLS (mTLS) has both sides present certificates. A service mesh such as Istio automates issuing and rotating per-service certificates and enforces policies on who may call whom.

worked.title: Carving a VPC and locking the database
steps: Start with a VPC range of 10.0.0.0/16, which holds 2^16 = 65,536 addresses.
Carve three /24 subnets, each with 2^8 = 256 addresses: public 10.0.1.0/24 (load balancer), app 10.0.2.0/24, data 10.0.3.0/24. Only the public subnet has a route to the internet.
Security group rules: the load balancer accepts port 443 from anywhere; the app accepts its port only from the load balancer's group; the database accepts port 5432 only from the app's group.
An attacker on the internet who learns the database address still cannot reach it: there is no route and no rule that allows them.
Add transport security: TLS terminates at the load balancer and is re-established to the app, and mTLS between services gives each caller an identity, such as the Kubernetes service account in Istio.
Add an authorisation rule: only the orders service identity may call the payments service. If the orders pod is compromised, the attacker still cannot call the user-admin service.
worked.result: From three small subnets and four rules, only one public door exists, and each tier can talk only to its direct neighbour, so one breach does not open everything.

case.title: BeyondCorp: no privileged internal network
case.text: Google's BeyondCorp paper starts from the observation that a perimeter firewall protects well until an attacker gets inside, after which they can move freely across a privileged internal network. With mobile devices and cloud services the perimeter is also harder to enforce. Google's answer was to drop the privileged internal network and move corporate applications to the internet, with access decided by the user and the device, not the network location. NIST later described the same idea as zero trust in SP 800-207, saying no implicit trust should come from network location or device ownership.

source.title: BeyondCorp: a new approach to enterprise security

A quick start, small low-risk systems

mistakes: Putting databases in public subnets, or allowing 0.0.0.0/0 to sensitive ports. Allow specific sources only.

Letting certificates expire. Automate issuance and rotation.
Keeping secrets in code, images or environment files in git. Use a secrets manager and rotate.
